newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Call for extension of SAfrica clothing duty scheme.
newsitem.headline: Call for extension of SAfrica clothing duty scheme.

text.p: Seardel Investment Corp Ltd chairman Aaron Searll has called for the duty credit certificate (DCC) scheme for the clothing industry to be extended to 2003 to support its export drive.

In his latest annual report, Searll said the present DCC expired in March 1998 and South Africa should follow the example of countries such as Australia which had similar schemes, but for up to 10 year periods.

"It is imperative that the existing scheme be extended forthwith to 2003 so that exporters are able to plan, with certainty, their future activities and not lose the export impetus that is currently being achieved," Searll said.
The DCC allows clothing exporters to offset 30 percent of the value of any one consignment of exports against the duty due on imports such as textiles.
Searll said he regretted, however, that DCC benefits had not been extended to "value added production on imported fabrics.
"Global sourcing by major retailers continues to increase in importance. Without this extension, South Africa will not be included in the global sourcing strategies of major retailers."

Searll said that following the renegotiation of the preferential trade agreement with Zimbabwe, it was now vital to develop a broader trade agreement covering all countries in the Southern African Development Community.
This should replace all current bilateral agreements which provided clothing from outside the region unfair access to South Africa through Malawi, Botswana, Namibia and Mozambique.
Searll said South Africa was "not being treated fairly" in the current free trade area negotiations with the European Union "despite the exhortations of friendship from Europe to South Africa."
He welcomed the formation of the customs law enforcement task group by government and the industry earlier this year to halt illegal imports.
"Thus far, some 400 tonnes of illegally imported textiles and clothing have been seized through these initiatives and six people have been arrested," Searll said.
